newsitem.title: Nigeria: Commonwealth welcomes Nigeria releases, wants more.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth welcomes Nigeria releases, wants more.

text.p: Commonwealth ministers on Wednesday ended a visit to persuade military ruled-Nigeria to restore democracy and respect civil rights by welcoming the freeing of three opposition activists and calling for more releases.
Lawyers Gani Fawehinmi, Femi Falana and Femi Aborishade, were freed unexpectedly on Tuesday as the seven Commonwealth ministers commenced their assignment in Abuja.

However, many other government opponents remain in detention, including Moshood Abiola, the businessman presumed to have won a 1993 presidential vote. The annulment of the election plunged Nigeria into political turmoil.

"We welcome the releases announced yesterday of three detained persons, who had been detained without trial and who were among those whose situations the Commonwealth has been concerned," Zimbabwean foreign minister Stan Mudenge and leader of the team told a news conference.
"We look forward to further releases," he added.

Sources at the talks said the military government was using a carrot-and-stick approach toward the Commonwealth team by releasing the three while blasting leading Commonwealth members Britain and Canada for their "anti-Nigeria stance."
"The Commonwealth is already split over Nigeria and it is obvious that the aim of the Nigerians is to maintain this split into the next summit," said one.
The next summit of the 53-member club of Britain and its former colonies is in Edinburgh, Scotland next year and is to decide whether or not to readmit Nigeria.
Africa's most populous nation is treated as a pariah for alleged human rights abuses and last year's hanging of nine minority rights activists from the Ogoni tribe, including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.
Those executions triggered establishment of the eight-member Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) to pressure Nigeria to restore civil rule and respect human rights.

A decision on whether to readmit Nigeria can only be taken by the Commonwealth summit on the recommendation of CMAG, which is made up of foreign ministers of Zimbabwe, Ghana, New Zealand, Jamaica, Britain, South Africa, Malaysia and Canada.
The CMAG ministers met military ruler General Sani Abacha late on Tuesday.
Their itinerary was agreed before the visit but Mudenge said Abacha told them they could see anyone and travel anywhere in Nigeria, including the volatile Ogoniland in the oil-producing southeast.
"But the time available to us during this visit did not make this possible on this occassion," he said. "We regret that we were unable to visit any detainees, including Chief Abiola."
Nigeria said the two-day Abuja meeting was a continuation of contacts that Nigeria hopes will lead to its readmission to the Commonwealth.

The CMAG ministers were briefed on Wednesday by party leaders, the electoral commission and the body implementing Abacha's programme to restore democracy in 1998 -- a period considered too long by domestic critics and the Commonwealth.
The ministers will meet again early next year.
